newsitem.title: USA: Long Beach copper stocks set to shrink further.
newsitem.headline: Long Beach copper stocks set to shrink further.

text.p: As Yasuo Hamanaka, the world's most infamous copper trader, reflects on life behind steel bars of a Tokyo detention center, his hold on a large hoard of metal far away on California's coast has slipped into red metal history, traders said.
Copper stockpiles in London Metal Exchange warehouses in Long Beach were widely seen as one of Hamanaka's key tools in gaining a mighty grip on the market.

The warehouses only opened in April 1995 but inventory rapidly shot up to almost 100,000 tonnes, a huge chunk of the London exchange's copper stocks, with most of the warrants held by Sumitomo Corp or Sumitomo-linked merchants such as Global Minerals and Metals.

"I think Sumitomo unquestionably had a large cache of Long Beach warrants until recently - I know because we bought some off them," a trader said. "If they are not all out of it, then they are pretty much out of it."
However, an official familiar with the main Californian warehouse, Metro International, said the company has not been requested to help official inquiries into the Sumitomo scandal.

Lawsuits filed in New York claimed that Sumitomo and others manipulated the market, and cited the company's accumulation of Long Beach stocks as the main device for allegedly rigging red metal prices.
Long Beach stocks have tumbled to 40,125 tonnes from 67,675 just before the Sumitomo scandal broke on June 13. About 37,000 tonnes are stored at Metro, the balance at California Cartage.

Warrants for metal at Metro are still fairly expensive at $15 to $20 because of what several brokers described as continuing logistical problems in taking metal out. Cartage warrants are much cheaper.

Brokers expected the drawdown of several thousand tonnes a week to continue, especially if the arbitrage, or premium of rival COMEX copper futures over LME, remains at the current wide 5 to 6 cents per pound for October and November.
"I think we are going to see a further 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes going out at least," a broker said.
A merchant added, "At the current pace, it would still take to January to get to zero, but I don't know if the arbitrage can last like this until then."
Ironically, many had predicted the end of wide arbitrage bands, if not the demise of the COMEX contract itself, by the opening of Long Beach LME warehouses.

Several market sources agreed that Long Beach metal was being shipped to three locations: COMEX warehouses in Tucson, Midwest consumers, and Far East consumers receiving deliveries from U.S. producers and traders.
The Far East or U.S. consumers presented the best deal because freight from Long Beach to Tucson costs twice as much as in the opposite direction, traders said.
Metro warehouse staff are working overtime to move out 1,200 to 1,400 tonnes of metal a day as warrant holders jostle for their metal, informed sources said.
Rumors also abound that metal stored at LME warehouses in Hamburg is crossing the water and heading for the United States, either to COMEX warehouses or to U.S. consumers.

"I don't believe these rumors because I know the fabricators and consumers. They have not been offered any," a trader said, adding that it would only make sense to ship Hamburg metal to U.S. consumers to obtain a physical premium rather than to COMEX where freight and duties would cut into the arbitrage.

The economics of shipping from Hamburg to a COMEX warehouse were doubtful at best, and would provoke thorny questions about possible manipulation of the arbitrage level between LME and COMEX, traders suggested.
